newsitem.title: USA: No request for US financing N.Korea deal - Cargill.
newsitem.headline: No request for US financing N.Korea deal - Cargill.

text.p: Cargill Inc has not asked the U.S. government to help finance a grain shipment to North Korea, and views the deal as strictly commercial, a Cargill official told Reuters on Tuesday.
"We've appproached this from the beginning as a commercial deal," said Cargill spokesperson Lori Johnson.

Cargill has been trying to work out an agreement with North Korea since early last month over the financing and other details of an approved 500,000-tonne grain shipment to the famine-stricken nation. Johnson said Cargill is hopeful an agreement will be hammered out soon.
North Korea is apparently attempting to use the negotiations with Cargill as a pawn in talks with U.S. officials on a U.S.-South Korea proposal for peace talks among those three countries and China.

The talks have been scheduled twice, but have been postponed each time by North Korean officials, who have said that before holding the meeting they want to successfully conclude the grain talks with Cargill.
North Korea is reportedly trying to put pressure on the U.S. government to help finance the grain deal in order to get the diplomatic talks moving.
Cargill's Johnson said that despite North Korea's efforts to link the grain negotiations and the political talks, the grain company is maintaining that it is not a part of the diplomatic debate.
"Obviously we're reading all the news accounts, but we're still not part of the diplomatic negotiations," said Johnson.
Johnson said that Cargill has kept the State Department informed on the status of the grain talks, but said this is "common precedure."
U.S. officials insisted Monday that Washington did not plan to intervene in the grain talks, for example by helping to finance North Korea's purchase.

The North Koreans "are obviously trying to link and leverage here," one official said. "We're not willing to play the game. They think we're so desperate to get this meeting, that maybe we'll put some money in the pot, and frankly we don't think that's necessary."
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns, however, held out the possibility that Washington might separately send food aid to North Korea, as it has done in the past.

He said Washington understood that the U.N. World Food Programme was considering making another emergency appeal for North Korea, and that if it did so, "...the United States will consider it very seriously."
South Korea's Red Cross, meanwhile, said it would send 700 metric tons of flour to the North on Tuesday, in addition to 300 tons shipped on Friday, a spokesman said.
North Korea said on Monday it has only half the grain it needs to feed its people because of two years of floods that destroyed crops.
